discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with IceCube
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led the construction of IceCube, a cubic-kilometre Cherenkov detector in the Antarctic ice, having first shown with AMANDA that the South Pole ice could serve as a neutrino telescope. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, a new messenger from the cosmos. It has since identified the first sources: the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017-18, with multimessenger follow-up), the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and neutrino emission from the Galactic plane (2023). These results rest on careful control of atmospheric backgrounds and detector systematics. They show that cosmic accelerators produce hadrons, bear on the origin of cosmic rays, and test neutrino physics at energies no laboratory can reach. This new observational window came from decades of instrument building and was carried through with statistical care. It has changed how we observe the high-energy universe.
